article_units.name: Computational Thinking
article_units.subtitle: Decomposition, abstraction, algorithms, trace tables, standard algorithms and truth tables

lessons.title: Decomposition, Abstraction and Subprograms
lessons.description: Breaking problems apart, hiding unnecessary detail and using subprograms to model the real world.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 Computational Thinking covers decomposition and abstraction — these concepts are universal. ~80% transferable. Edexcel explicitly adds the BENEFITS OF SUBPROGRAMS as a 1.1.2 sub-topic (reusability, testing in isolation, reducing complexity, division of labour). Add a short worked example showing decomposition into named subprograms. Drop AQA's framing about algorithm-vs-program distinction (Edexcel does not stress this in the same way). Regenerate exam-tip toward Edexcel's Explain (2-4 marks) and Discuss (6 marks) command words.

lessons.title: Algorithms: Flowcharts, Pseudocode and Constructs
lessons.description: Reading and writing algorithms with sequence, selection, repetition and iteration using flowcharts and pseudocode.
section_markers: flowchart symbols start end process decision input output predefined subprogram
arithmetic operators modulus integer division exponentiation

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 covers pseudocode and flowcharts but uses AQA's standard pseudo-code reference. Edexcel takes a deliberately informal stance — its spec footnote says pseudocode is 'an informal written description of a program' with no strict syntax requirement. Rewrite all worked examples in plain English pseudocode (no FOR..ENDFOR style). Use the six Edexcel flowchart symbols from Appendix 2 (start/end terminator, process, input/output, decision, flow arrow, predefined subprogram). Bundle the operators here so the next lesson can focus on tracing. Examiner reports flag students describing the > operator incorrectly and outputting yes/no rather than Boolean — drill correct Boolean output.

lessons.title: Trace Tables, Error Types and Algorithm Evaluation
lessons.description: Tracing algorithms by hand, identifying syntax, logic and runtime errors, and judging fitness for purpose.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Trace table technique transfers wholesale from AQA L2. Add an explicit error-types section: examiner report 2024 flagged that many candidates 'gave definitions that were vague or ambiguous' for syntax errors and confused them with logic or runtime errors. Drill the precise definition: 'a syntax error means the rules of a programming language have been broken'. Add Edexcel-specific algorithm-efficiency framing (compares, passes through loop, memory use) — this is in 1.2.7 and gets examined as an Explain (4 marks) question.

lessons.title: Standard Algorithms: Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Linear and Binary Search
lessons.description: How the four standard algorithms work, when each is appropriate and how to compare their efficiency.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 (search) and L4 (sort) merge cleanly into one Edexcel lesson — the spec lists all four standard algorithms together in 1.2.6. ~85% transferable. Use Edexcel's Describe (2-4 marks) and Explain command-word framing for practice questions instead of AQA's Compare-and-Contrast. Walkthrough sequences (e.g. bubble sort passes, binary search halving) reuse cleanly. Drop AQA's note that 'no formal big-O' — same applies for Edexcel but no need to flag it explicitly.

lessons.title: Truth Tables and Logical Operators
lessons.description: Building truth tables with AND, OR and NOT for up to three inputs and using logic to solve problems.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 of Computer Systems covers Boolean logic but bundles in XOR gates, logic circuit diagrams and Boolean expression notation (. + overbar). Edexcel does NOT examine XOR, does NOT examine logic circuit diagrams or symbols, and does NOT require Boolean expression notation. Edexcel only requires building truth tables with AND/OR/NOT for up to three inputs. Score is 'low' because most of AQA's content gets dropped — keep only the AND/OR/NOT truth-table mechanics and reframe around 'using logic to solve problems'. Build the lesson around step-by-step truth-table construction for compound expressions (e.g. (A AND B) OR (NOT C)).

article_units.name: Data
article_units.subtitle: Binary, two's complement, hexadecimal, character encoding, images, sound, storage units and compression

lessons.title: Binary Numbers, Two's Complement and Hexadecimal
lessons.description: Representing positive and negative integers in binary, converting between bases and using hexadecimal.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 covers binary and hex conversions universally. ~60% transferable. Major difference: Edexcel explicitly requires TWO'S COMPLEMENT for signed integers (range -128 to +127); AQA 8525 does not assess two's complement. Need a fresh worked example for two's complement conversion (e.g. -5 in 8-bit two's complement). Hex conversion technique transfers wholesale. Drop AQA's binary addition of three numbers (Edexcel only specifies addition of TWO positive binary patterns — that goes in the next lesson).

lessons.title: Binary Arithmetic and Shifts
lessons.description: Adding binary numbers, applying logical and arithmetic shifts, and recognising overflow.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 covers binary addition and logical shifts but Edexcel adds two distinct shift types: LOGICAL shifts (zero fill) AND ARITHMETIC shifts (preserve sign bit). AQA does not assess arithmetic shifts. Add a worked example for both. Overflow is examined in both boards but Edexcel asks for an UNDERSTANDING of overflow as a concept (1-2 marks Define/Explain) rather than detecting it in a calculation.

lessons.title: Characters, Images and Sound
lessons.description: Encoding text with 7-bit ASCII and representing bitmap images and sampled sound in binary.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 covers images and sound representation universally. Edexcel uses 7-bit ASCII only (no Unicode requirement in 2.2.1) whereas AQA L2 covers both — drop the Unicode section. Image file-size calculations transfer cleanly. Examiner report 2024 flagged that 'many responses correctly identified height x width but failed to specify the units in pixels' — drill the pixels-as-unit rule. Sound calculations transfer wholesale. Add a paragraph on the LIMITATIONS of binary representation when bits are constrained (2.2.4) — this is Edexcel-specific framing.

lessons.title: Storage Units, File Sizes and Compression
lessons.description: Binary multiples kibibyte through tebibyte, file-size calculations and lossy vs lossless compression.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Score is 'low' because Edexcel and AQA diverge significantly here. Edexcel uses BINARY multiples (kibibyte = 1024 bytes, mebibyte, gibibyte, tebibyte) — AQA 8525 explicitly uses DECIMAL SI prefixes (kB = 1000 bytes). Examiner report 2024: 'many candidates did not manage to correctly identify how many bytes are in a tebibyte' — drill the 1024^n progression. Compression: Edexcel only assesses lossy vs lossless as concepts; AQA 8525 examines Huffman trees and RLE explicitly. Drop Huffman and RLE entirely. Fresh worked example needed for tebibyte calculation.

article_units.name: Computers
article_units.subtitle: Hardware, CPU architecture, secondary storage, operating systems and programming languages

lessons.title: CPU, Main Memory and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
lessons.description: The von Neumann model, main memory, the CPU components and how each instruction is fetched, decoded and executed.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 covers the CPU and fetch-decode-execute cycle. ~65% transferable. Key difference: Edexcel EXPLICITLY assesses the von Neumann stored-program concept (3.1.1) and the THREE BUSES (address, data, control). AQA does not require buses by name. Add a labelled walkthrough showing how each bus is used during fetch/decode/execute. Keep AQA's reminder that the cycle has three stages — examiner reports flag students conflating fetch-decode-execute into 'fetch-execute'. Drop AQA's performance factors (clock speed, cores, cache) — Edexcel does not examine these here.

lessons.title: Secondary Storage and Embedded Systems
lessons.description: How data is stored on magnetic, optical and solid-state media, and what makes a system embedded.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 (Memory and Storage) covers secondary storage and embedded systems. ~80% transferable. Drop AQA's RAM/ROM/cache content (those go in L1 here under main memory). Keep magnetic/optical/SSD trade-offs wholesale. Embedded systems definition + examples transfer cleanly. Drop AQA's cloud storage section — Edexcel does not assess cloud storage in 3.1.

lessons.title: Operating Systems, Utility Software and Robust Software
lessons.description: What an OS does, what utility programs run alongside it, and how developers identify vulnerabilities.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 covers OS and utility software but bundles in programming languages. Edexcel splits OS/utilities from programming languages — keep them split here. Edexcel adds a specific 'robust software' sub-topic (3.2.3) covering audit trails and code reviews as ways to identify vulnerabilities — this is fresh content not in AQA. Build that section around the design-time techniques (code reviews) vs runtime techniques (audit trails). Drop AQA's hardware-vs-software definition (already implicit).

lessons.title: Programming Languages: High-level, Low-level, Compilers and Interpreters
lessons.description: The characteristics of high- and low-level languages and how interpreters and compilers translate code differently.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4's second half covers translators — transfers cleanly. ~85% transferable. Edexcel only assesses interpreters vs compilers (3.3.2) — drop AQA's assembler content. Use Edexcel's Describe (2-4 marks) and Explain (2-4 marks) command words for practice. Standard table comparing interpreter vs compiler (translation timing, error detection, distribution of executable, portability) is a frequent exam item.

article_units.name: Networks
article_units.subtitle: Network types, the internet, protocols, the four-layer TCP/IP model, topologies and network security

lessons.title: Networks, the Internet and Connectivity
lessons.description: Why we connect computers, the difference between LAN and WAN, how the internet is structured, and wired vs wireless trade-offs.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 (Networks and Protocols) covers LAN/WAN and wired/wireless trade-offs. ~60% transferable. Edexcel does NOT examine PAN (drop). Edexcel adds explicit calculation expressions for transmission time (file size / rate) — this is examined as a Calculate (2-4 marks) question, which AQA does not require. Internet structure (IP addressing, routers) is examined more explicitly in Edexcel than AQA. Drop AQA's protocols list from this lesson — Edexcel covers protocols in a separate lesson.

lessons.title: Network Protocols and the TCP/IP Model
lessons.description: Why protocols exist, the standard internet and email protocols, and how the four-layer TCP/IP model handles data.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 (Network Security and TCP/IP) covers the four-layer TCP/IP model — transfers wholesale. ~85% transferable. KEY DIFFERENCE: Edexcel's protocol list INCLUDES FTP and POP3 (POP3 is NOT in AQA 8525's list anymore). Add FTP (file transfer) and POP3 (email retrieve, deletes from server). Also add Ethernet and Wi-Fi as protocols — Edexcel lists these alongside the others. Examiner report 2024: 'Few candidates discussed MAC addresses and how they are used at the link layer. Many candidates confused the link layer with the network layer and IP addressing.' Drill the layer-to-protocol mapping carefully.

lessons.title: Network Topologies
lessons.description: How computers are physically and logically connected in bus, star and mesh layouts, and the trade-offs of each.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA 8525 does NOT examine network topologies. Edexcel 4.1.8 specifically requires bus, star and mesh — this is Edexcel-unique content. Build from scratch with three labelled topology diagrams and a comparison table on cost/reliability/scalability/ease of adding nodes. Drop ring topology (not in spec). Practice question style: Describe a topology (2-4 marks), Explain a trade-off (2-4 marks).

lessons.title: Network Security
lessons.description: Identifying vulnerabilities with penetration testing and ethical hacking, and protecting networks with access control and firewalls.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2's network security section overlaps but AQA focuses on encryption, authentication and MAC filtering. Edexcel 4.2.1 emphasises penetration testing and ethical hacking as IDENTIFICATION methods, and access control, physical security and firewalls as PROTECTION methods. Restructure as identify-vs-protect. Drop encryption (Edexcel covers it in topic 5.3 cybersecurity instead). Add a brief paragraph on the ethics of penetration testing (with permission vs without).

article_units.name: Issues and Impact
article_units.subtitle: Environmental impact, ethical and legal issues, AI accountability, intellectual property and cybersecurity

lessons.title: Environmental, Ethical and Legal Issues
lessons.description: The energy cost of digital devices, e-waste, privacy and data protection, and intellectual property law.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 (Ethical and Legal Issues) overlaps on privacy and IP but bundles autonomous vehicles. Edexcel separates these — autonomous vehicles is in 5.2.2 (next lesson). Environmental section (5.1.1) is brief in Edexcel — energy, manufacture, replacement cycle, disposal — combine with ethical/legal here for a strong unit lesson. Edexcel splits IP into four categories (copyright, patents, trademarks, licencing) and examines each as distinct. Add brief explainers of each. Drop AQA's autonomous-vehicles content and mobile/wearable tech.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Robotics
lessons.description: Accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and legal liability for AI and autonomous systems.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 (Autonomous Vehicles and Environmental Impacts) covers self-driving cars. Edexcel 5.2.2 is broader: AI, machine learning AND robotics, with four named ethical issues (accountability, safety, algorithmic bias, legal liability). Build the lesson around those four issues with a worked example for each (e.g. algorithmic bias = COMPAS recidivism case framed generically without naming specific datasets). Self-driving cars become ONE example of robotics here, not the whole lesson. Discuss (6-mark) practice question fits this topic perfectly per Edexcel's command-word taxonomy.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity: Threats and Protection
lessons.description: How malware, social engineering and exploits attack digital systems, and the layered defences that protect them.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 (Cyber Security Threats) covers malware and social engineering. ~65% transferable. Edexcel 5.3.1 has a WIDER malware list — adds worms, ransomware, key loggers (AQA tightly limits to virus/trojan/spyware). Use Edexcel's full list. Edexcel 5.3.2 names exactly five protections (anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup, recovery) — restructure as the five protections. Drop AQA-specific terms like 'blagging', 'shouldering' (Edexcel keeps social engineering at a higher level). Add a worked example of a layered defence strategy combining all five.

article_units.name: Programming with Python
article_units.subtitle: Reading, writing and refining Python programs using the Programming Language Subset

lessons.title: Program Structure, Data Types and Variables
lessons.description: The building blocks of a Python program: constants, variables, primitive data types and assignment statements.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 (Data Types and Constructs) covers primitives and constructs — ~60% transferable. Major difference: Edexcel is PYTHON-SPECIFIC. Rewrite all examples in Python 3 using PLS conventions (no FOR..ENDFOR pseudocode). Edexcel calls reals 'real' (matches AQA) but examines char vs string as DISTINCT primitives. Add the four readability techniques from spec 6.1.4 (layout, indentation, comments, meaningful identifiers, white space) early — examiner reports flag students who over-comment ('the number of comments exceeded the number of code lines') so model comments at start of code blocks rather than per-line.

lessons.title: Selection, Repetition and Iteration in Python
lessons.description: Writing if-elif-else, while and for loops, and iterating over the items in a list or string.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 (Iteration, Selection and Operators) covers the three constructs but in pseudocode and across all four iteration types (WHILE, REPEAT-UNTIL, DO-WHILE, FOR). Edexcel is Python-only — use only `for` (count-controlled and iteration over collection) and `while` (condition-controlled). Drop REPEAT-UNTIL and DO-WHILE — Python doesn't have them. Worked examples: classic if-elif-else menu, for-range loop with accumulator, while loop with sentinel input. Drop AQA's operator section (operators get their own lesson here).

lessons.title: Operators and String Manipulation
lessons.description: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators in Python, plus length, position, substring and case-conversion operations.
section_markers: arithmetic operators addition subtraction division multiplication

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 (Arrays, Records and String Handling) covers string operations and AQA L2 covers operators — combine here. ~80% transferable. Use Python operator syntax (// for integer division, % for modulus, ** for exponentiation). String operations use Python conventions (len(s), s[0], s[1:4], s.upper(), s.lower(), + for concatenation). Drop AQA's char-to-code/code-to-char (not in Edexcel). Examiner report 2024 flagged that students described relational operators incorrectly — drill correct Boolean output (True/False, not yes/no).

lessons.title: Lists, Arrays, Records and 2D Structures
lessons.description: Working with one- and two-dimensional arrays, lists and records to organise structured data.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L4 covers arrays and records. ~55% transferable. Edexcel works in Python — use lists (1D arrays) and nested lists (2D arrays). Records in Python conventionally use dictionaries or simple class definitions but the PLS allows either — show the dictionary approach as simplest. Add a worked 2D-list traversal example (e.g. a 3x3 grid). Drop AQA's RECORD..ENDRECORD pseudocode entirely. Iterating over a 2D structure with nested loops is a frequent Paper 2 exam item.

lessons.title: Input, Output, Files and Validation
lessons.description: Reading user input, working with CSV files, and writing validation and authentication routines.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA 8525 does NOT assess file I/O at GCSE — explicit AQA spec exclusion. Edexcel REQUIRES reading and writing CSV files (6.4.2). This is a major Edexcel-unique topic. Build from scratch with a Python CSV worked example: open in read mode, iterate rows, open in write mode, write a header and rows. Validation (length/presence/range/pattern) maps to AQA's robust programming but Edexcel adds pattern check (regex-style) — note PLS allows simple pattern matching, no need for full regex. Authentication: simple ID/password lookup against a file or in-memory list.

lessons.title: Subprograms, Scope and Debugging
lessons.description: Writing procedures and functions with parameters, using local and global variables, and locating program errors.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 (Subroutines, Parameters and Local Variables) covers subprograms. ~65% transferable. Edexcel distinguishes FUNCTIONS (must return a value, parameters optional) from PROCEDURES (no return value, parameters optional) — be precise. Use Python def syntax with explicit return for functions and no return for procedures. Add scope: parameters and variables defined inside def are local; module-level variables can be accessed inside subprograms but reassigning needs global. Bundle debugging here from 6.1.5/6.1.6 — combine with test data and program evaluation. Examiner-report finding: students gave vague definitions of syntax errors. Drill exact definitions.

unique_to_source.lesson: L1 Boolean Logic and Truth Tables (XOR + logic circuit diagrams + Boolean expression notation)

unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Edexcel 2.3.2 only requires understanding of lossy vs lossless as concepts. Huffman trees and RLE worked examples are AQA-only.

unique_to_source.lesson: L1-L3 Relational Databases and SQL (all three lessons)

unique_to_source.lesson: L4 Detecting and Preventing Cyber Threats (biometrics, CAPTCHA, email confirmation)
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Edexcel 5.3.2 names exactly five protections (anti-malware, encryption, AUP, backup, recovery). Biometrics, CAPTCHA and email confirmation are AQA-specific framings.

unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Edexcel 2.2.1 only assesses 7-bit ASCII. Unicode and UTF-8/UTF-16 are not in Edexcel.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that a syntax error is 'a spelling mistake' or 'a grammar mistake' in isolation. Examiners reject this as ambiguous because it could equally describe a logic error. The correct definition is that a syntax error means the rules of the programming language have been broken.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked the output of a relational expression such as a > b, students give 'yes/no' rather than 'True/False'. Examiners require the Boolean output type.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students correctly write height × width × colour depth but omit the unit 'pixels' for height and width. The unit is required for marks. Some students also include colour depth when only width × height is asked for, and vice versa.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse tebibytes (1024^4 bytes, binary) with terabytes (10^12 bytes, decimal) and miss the kibi/mebi/gibi/tebi progression. Many cannot correctly state how many bytes are in a tebibyte. Edexcel uses BINARY multiples (1024-based).
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1 + specification 2.3.1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked to name a network protocol, some students give a file format such as .mp3 or .jpg. Protocols are rules for communication (HTTP, TCP, IMAP), not file types.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.topic: TCP/IP link layer vs network layer
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the link layer (which deals with MAC addresses and the physical network medium) with the internet/network layer (which deals with IP addresses and routing). Few candidates can describe MAC addresses' role at the link layer.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students comment every line of Python, sometimes producing more comment lines than code lines. Examiners want comments to explain the LOGIC, placed at the start of blocks of code — not per-line restatements of what the code obviously does.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2022, Paper 2, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students try to use AQA-style or OCR-style pseudocode (FOR..ENDFOR, ←). Edexcel's spec footnote is clear that pseudocode is 'an informal written description of a program' with NO strict syntax requirement — plain English is acceptable.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Specification, footnote to topic 1.2, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students compress the three-stage cycle into 'fetch and execute' and omit the decode stage. The spec explicitly states three stages in 3.1.1.
Students use the terms function and procedure interchangeably. Edexcel 6.6.2 is precise: a function MUST return a value, a procedure must NOT return a value. Both may or may not take parameters.

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Vague or ambiguous definitions that could apply to multiple terms — for example, defining a syntax error as 'a mistake' which equally describes a logic or runtime error. Use the exact spec phrasing where possible.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Students give a description (statement of fact) instead of an explanation (statement of fact + reasoning or consequence). Examiner mark scheme requires each marking point to be linked to a justification.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Complete a Trace Table: Students add extra rows for iterations that didn't happen, or skip the update of a counter variable across rows. Drill the discipline of one row per state change.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Discuss: Students list arguments on one side only. The Discuss command word requires identifying the issue, exploring ALL aspects, and investigating by reasoning. Use a two-sided structure with evaluation.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Complete an Algorithm: Students lose marks for incomplete control flow, missing loop termination, or wrong output. Practise scaffolding: identify inputs, define the process step-by-step, define the output, then write.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Write a Subprogram: Common errors: function does not return a value when required; parameters are not used inside the body; identifier names don't match those in the calling code. Practise signature-first, body-second, return-third.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper 1 (50%, 75 marks, 1h 30m) covers topics 1–5 with one question per topic. Topic balance is roughly equal across the five questions but topic 1 (computational thinking) and topic 6 (programming) carry the cognitive load of the whole qualification.
Paper 2 (50%, 75 marks, 2h, onscreen Python) is six compulsory questions all drawn from topic 6. Half the course's lesson time should sit on programming.
Examiner reports consistently flag the data-representation calculations (tebibytes, image file sizes) as low-scoring — allocate strong worked examples here.
The four-layer TCP/IP model and protocol mapping are examined every year as 4–6 marks — drill the layer-to-protocol matching.
Cybersecurity (5.3) is split into threats (5.3.1) and protections (5.3.2) — both appear in every Paper 1 series, typically 4–6 marks.

Paper 2 Amend questions (5–15 marks) require students to read existing code and modify it. Paper 2 Write questions (5–15 marks) require fresh code. Both command words appear every series — practise both.
current_spec_changes: The Programming Language Subset (PLS) is updated annually. Version 6 (Summer 2025) clarified the two supported list dimensions and amended string.format and built-in subprogram descriptions. The latest PLS version is the authoritative reference for what Python features are examinable.
Python 3 is the only assessed language for Paper 2. The specification mentions that any version of a Python 3 interpreter is acceptable.
Specification first teaching was September 2020, first certification 2022. No major spec rewrites since. The Programming Language Subset is the only document that updates annually.
pedagogical_notes: EEF cognitive science evidence review (2021) supports worked examples as the highest-impact strategy for new programming content. Each programming lesson should walk through a fully-coded example before the practice section asks students to write their own.

PRIMM (Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make) is the most-cited pedagogy for GCSE programming. Particularly effective for Paper 2 Amend questions, where students must read existing code before modifying it. Use predict-then-trace as a routine for new code snippets.

EEF guidance on retrieval practice (2024 blog series) recommends spaced, conceptual retrieval rather than recognition. Knowledge checks should use fill-in-the-blank and short-answer formats for key vocabulary (Boolean, syntax error, kibibyte) rather than multiple choice for definitions.

EEF FAME framework for worked examples (alternation, fading, modelling, examining) maps directly onto programming pedagogy: alternate worked examples with similar problems, fade scaffolding as students gain confidence.
Dual coding pairs well with trace tables, flowcharts and TCP/IP layer diagrams. Use a visual paired with prose for any algorithm or networking concept.

Edexcel's spec is deliberately informal about pseudocode (an explicit footnote in 1.2). Content should mirror this — show plain-English step-by-step descriptions, not a formal pseudocode dialect, so students don't lose marks by misremembering syntax they were never required to learn.
